utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. This is case number IT-97-24-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I please have the appearances of the OTP, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Branko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, can you follow the proceedings in a language you understand? THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just in order that it's not forgotten by the end of the day, do you have any health problems or are there any contributions you want to make as regards the conditions in the detention unit? THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] I have no health problems for the time being, and I have nothing else to say at this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, I have to inform all participants that we need to have a break at 3.00. The Judges will be sworn in. This is just Judge Fassi Fihri, assigned to this case, and Judge Per Lindholm from Finland who arrived yesterday in the Simic case, and therefore I think it's really necessary to be there. We will have a break for 20 to 30 minutes from then on, from 3.00. Thank you. As you have seen from all the documents, and even from the newspapers, finally this Tribunal succeeded in obtaining the necessary budget that this case can be started; that there is the possibility of the Office of the Prosecutor to present the case, and the possibility for the accused and the Defence to prepare the Defence case and to be heard in due time. And I am grateful knowing very well all the problems we are facing, the OTP, the Defence, and the Trial Chamber itself, that we really can start this case now next Tuesday, and then that we can have this Pre-Trial Conference today. You have received the scheduling order stating all the envisaged courtroom days as from next Tuesday to August 2. I would appreciate if there is any obstacle for anybody present, to tell it immediately. And if there would be a new obstacle in future, please tell it in advance, so that the Office of the Prosecutor and the Registry can take care, especially when it's a question of incoming witnesses. Are there any obstacles for the OTP? I know it's difficult having Brdjanin and Talic running and Stakic running at the same time, sometimes in the morning, some times parallelly, and sometimes morning and evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it would obviously be preferable from our point of view if this case could run in the morning and Brdjanin and Talic in the afternoon, but I haven't looked at the two. I know for most of the time, the two cases are actually running at the same time. Any problem which may arise at the moment is that next Tuesday, Your Honour will be expecting me to open the case; in addition, there is a witness which I have to call in the Brdjanin/Talic case, and it may be that that Trial Chamber will be inconvenienced as a result. Other than that, Your Honour, what I can say is Your Honour knows that we are anxious to try and combine the witnesses here with the Brdjanin/Talic case, and on the trial schedule that Your Honours set out, and the one in the Brdjanin/Talic case at the moment, there's no meeting. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, the Trial Chamber is aware of these problems, and I can tell you that in the [indiscernible], this had been part of a strong and in depth debate, but we have to take into account also the problems of other cases. Normally the case of Galic is heard in this room, and at the end of the day, we didn't find any other comprise, and it's a comprise we have now in all the six Trial Chambers, and the interests of the Office of the Prosecutor, the Defence counsel, and so on, therefore I can tell you that there will, indeed, be a kind of flexibility in both cases when it's really necessary. The question of the hearing of parallel witnesses to be heard in Brdjanin/Talic and in Stakic, this should be discussed later this day, because I think it's a real crucial point. Only the question whether or not there were obstacles as regards to concrete dates until the 3rd of August. There are no general remarks from your side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no obstacles on the Defence side, so we are ready to proceed as scheduled, for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then I have first of all a general question to the Defence. And of course, also, to the accused. We have two counsel in this case, you, Mr. Branko Lukic, and Mr. Zdravko Ostojic. As I understand, Mr. Ostojic will arrive next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. Ostojic will be here in Den Haag on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That bad experience of last week brings me to put the question forward to you: Are you prepared to be the only Defence counsel in case Mr. Ostojic will not be present?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am prepared; but hopefully, he will be here. I don't have any news that he is going to quit this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And would it be also -- is there your consent that in case, for unforeseen reasons, you, yourself, are not available, that Mr. Ostojic substitutes you for this period of time? We'll say that Mr. Ostojic alone is representing the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind and ask Mr. Ostojic to provide me with the same information in writing until the 16th of April, that he is prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- to take over the role of the Defence alone?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have, of course, to ask Mr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic, do you agree that in the case of the absence of one Defence counsel, only one Defence counsel is present? THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I haven't consulted my Defence about this, but I believe that if the time in question is short, like a day or two, that could be acceptable. But please allow me some time, until the 15th or the 16th, to consult my Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be possible for you to discuss this question in short with your Defence counsel during the next break, after 3.00? THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] I think I can do that, and I will have a position to present to you after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come back to you, and you may be seated. As regards now, the agenda of today, I will propose the following: That we start first with bits and pieces related to the indictment. Once again, that we then go on to the question of the witnesses, the question of depositions, admission of evidence and identification. Then, other, as it was said, related matters, the right of the accused to be heard. Then matters not in dispute; the question of contested matters of fact and law; the question of tendering of exhibits; whether or not there should be a time limit for cross-examination; issues on protective measures; some questions related to translations; the opening of the trial. We'll say the first days from Tuesday to Friday, next week, and then to touch upon outstanding motions. Are there any other general issues you mentioned you want to raise today? Any other issues? Or are you satisfied?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is -- I'm just wondering whether Your Honour was going to open the case from Tuesday to Friday. I'm sorry, I'll say it again. Your Honour says the first days, from Tuesday to Friday, the opening of the trial, I don't think it's going to take me four days to open this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In a broader sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I say for one, which relates to numbering of exhibits in advance, for a reason I'll explain to Your Honour when we get to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, the question of Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Which, of course, will be included, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: From the side of the Defence team, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had a pretty constructive meeting yesterday with the senior legal officer, and we, I think, clarified a lot of things. So I have nothing new for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we can start with point number 1, the amended indictment, which of course has to be read together with the Pre-Trial brief, together with the list of witnesses, together with the summary of witnesses, together with the charter of proof provided by the Office of the Prosecutor. I think numerous problems will be resolved when we read the entire package together. Before I come to the still-pending motion objecting to the form of the indictment, I want to raise ex officio some tiny points. It was already discussed yesterday that in paragraph 56, the counts 6 -- 7 and 8 have to be substituted by 10 and 11. It was agreed. And I think it was also agreed that there would be a new attachment of the list of the names of the victims as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, can I formally apply in respect of -- rather than bringing this by written motion, to amend paragraph 56 to read, instead of counts 10 and 11, 7 and 8. In addition to that, if Your Honour looks at paragraph 54 -- sorry, paragraph 54 [3], yes, and then little numbers, we went in the listing of the religious institutions. We went from 9 through to 12. We would like to amend so that it reads "9, 10, and 11."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you please repeat. You said in 54 [3].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, if you look at page 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'll see there's a list of the various Catholic churches, mosques, et cetera. I don't know what went wrong. But you'll see we go 7, 8, 9, then 12, 13. We should be going "9, 10, 11." So I would like to formally apply to amend that as well. I'm going to produce a new typed version. Your Honour, in respect of the schedule of victims, we've got it. We'll put it in. But Your Honour, I'm not very happy about it. I know Judge Rodrigues ordered it. But if we start listing people who we say were killed, we're going to get into all sorts of problems. We can prove that numbers 1, 9, 10, and 11 were killed. I'm simply asking, Your Honour, whether it's necessary. We're going to be leading evidence of people being killed. Is there any real necessity for it to be listed in a schedule like this? We did actually leave it out deliberately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, but if I see the jurisprudence of this Tribunal until now correctly, there are admittedly different approaches. But I really think it's preferable to have this list. And I know about the problems linked to this, but when balancing is -- I can tell you whatever I discuss today, this has already been discussed with the new ad litem Judges which will form the Bench. To make it quite clear, we have, of course, the problem under the Statute and under the Rules as it stands now, that until next Tuesday, all decisions have to be taken by the permanent Judges. But it's, of course, relevant for the incoming ad litem Judges. We have to work together for the next month on this case. And therefore, I discussed it in advance with these Judges. There is an amendment pending that also the ad litem Judges are allowed to participate in Pre-Trial work in future, but unfortunately it is not yet applicable, and therefore I discussed these issues in advance. And we came to the conclusion that it would be preferable to have this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and may I say I don't feel very strongly about it, but this is one of the cases referred to by Judge Hunt, because effectively we have rewritten the jurisprudence on this matter. But it's not suggested that this defendant, accused, is responsible for any of these killings, and I think there's a difference between an allegation made against an accused who is directly responsible for the killings, and someone who is in a position of authority. And we say as such, is responsible. My only concern is, if this schedule is attached to and forms part of the indictment, for some reason or another, we don't prove that, for example, the first named -- let's take, for example, a long list of people, taken from the Keraterm and Omarska camps. We are not intending, because we want to keep this trial within manageable proportions to call every single witness who could prove that each and every one of these people were killed. So in the end, if this becomes part of the indictment, we're going to have to strike names through possibly. But Your Honour, I don't feel that strongly about it. Just as a matter of principle, whether it's actually necessary. And Your Honour and Your Honour's colleagues discussed it, feel it is, that's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful. We know your problem, but we believe that it can be resolved during trial should there be any obstacle of the nature you just mentioned. One serious concern is Count 1 and 2 as they stand now. In paragraph 51, you plead "Count 1, genocide," then going on, "and/or, Count 2, complicity in genocide." It is my understanding that it is impossible to commit genocide and complicity in genocide. Therefore, not only in my mine, but in our point of view, it would be preferable to plead as it was done in other cases in the last month, to plead Count 1 (a), genocide, or alternatively, Count 1 (b) complicity in genocide. I would be more than happy if you could agree with this language.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that as a matter of law, I don't see how you can be both guilty of genocide and complicity, but there is a certain amount of discussion because of the wide-ranging nature of these events. And I think most of the indictments that I'm aware of have pleaded it as "and/or."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Newest version, I'm afraid it's in the last time in this year, the new indictments are always pleaded "or alternatively," and then 1 (a), 1 (b).

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they are different offences. It would be Count 1 or Count 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, or even to make it quite clear, it was done in the last indictment, to say "1 (a)," or "1 (ii)," not to give the wrong impression that there would be two different counts at the end of the day. There could really be two charges and two decisions on both unparallely or communitively.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, I think there is some merit in Your Honour's suggestion because in fact, Counts 3, 4, and 5 are either -- they are "and/or" if you see what I mean. You could be guilty of genocide plus the rest, and then sentenced. So Your Honour would it like it to be Count 1 (a) genocide or Count 1 (b) complicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Or alternatively, Count 1 (b), complicity and genocide.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can do that. But it will throw out the Pre-Trial brief numbering, if Your Honour sees that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We will apply the Pre-Trial brief correspondingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Another point is coming to paragraph 46, I believe it is. Here you have -- you quote a certain number of camps. In the former indictment, there were only three camps. Just for the purposes of clarification, it should be pointed out whether or not there are now additional camps, and I want to make reference to your Pre-Trial brief under paragraph 56. You want again, the three camps that were included in the former indictment, and "Keraterm, Omarska, Trnopolje," and as it is the language there "other camps." So could you please grant us a little bit of clarification. Do you intend to say under, of course, one and the same charge. No doubt about this, we have to take into account and to include also other camps?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the major camps are obviously Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje. But when we reread this, we realised that witnesses were going to be talking about other, more transitory camps, if one likes to put it -- less permanent. So we thought it only right to list them in the indictment. When the Pre-Trial brief was looked at, we didn't bother to do it. But our view was that in amending this indictment, we should give as much information as we could. And we will be calling evidence from people about incarceration in these other three places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I understand you correctly that your intention is to say that other camps, in paragraph 56 of the Pre-Trial brief, these are those under 46. There the notion of "camp" is not used, but Prijedor, JNA barracks, Miska Glava community centre, and SUP building in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Under the term of "camp," we understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is also clear for you? Thank you, for this clarification. I'll come back to this point immediately after the break. And if you could be so kind to discuss the question of the Defence with your client right now, then I think we should try to restart within 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Simply having dealt with the amendments we've applied for, and the one that Your Honour has ordered to, in other words to attach the schedule, is Your Honour granting them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think Your Honour said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No. Quite clear. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you once again for giving us the possibility to participate in the solemn declaration of the three new ad litem Judges. One step further to the beginning of our trial. We discussed and had the necessary clarification on paragraph 46 as regards the notion of camps. And then also for clarification purposes on the same charges, there is a new location added, Ljubija football stadium. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could Your Honour just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Paragraph 46, we discussed right now. And in paragraph 49, there is a new location, the Ljubija football stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, in addition, if we could have a look together on paragraph 44, the former 45, now we have not number of man as it was before, but number of people. Evidently, it is your intention to include -- and it of course makes sense in the entire context -- to include men, women, children. That was your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then you added the village of Biscani and surrounding areas. Is there any possibility to have a little bit of clarifications what you regard as "surrounding areas of Biscani"?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, not with a complete map coordination, no, but it means that some of the people were killed not in the actual village itself, but in the outlying fields and the like. I mean we're talking within the radius, and we'll make it clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There will be maps which will show what the various areas are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then we may probably come to the last point of concern. Of course, it's also for the Defence to come with one or another point. But in paragraph 27, the former paragraph 20, apparently there is an exchange of dates. In the former version, under paragraph 20 [A], it was alleged that the crime was committed prior to the declaration of the assembly of 17 January, 1992. And then, going on, "the enterprise existed at least until 30 September, 1992." Now, we can read that the starting point is 24 October, and this needs some declaration, "this joint criminal enterprise continued throughout the period of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the signing of the Dayton accords in 1995." Here, for me, it seems to be, yes, a significant change of the period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this case is a smaller part of the Brdjanin/Talic and Krajisnik/Plavsic and eventually the Milosevic case. There is the joint enterprise, we say, throughout, that the whole period, from the evidence, began not later than the 1st assembly of the Serbian people, which was in October, and continued through until the end of the conflict enforced upon the participants by the Dayton accords. We're not suggesting that Stakic's part in it is any greater in the original indictment, but the enterprise we say is one enterprise, and that is the reason why it is now -- it's the same in all of the indictments. That's the period. Stakic played his part in that enterprise. We're looking for consistency, and that's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand that you regard the time frame for the entire alleged joint criminal enterprise as from October 1991 until 1995. Not to be misunderstood, is it alleged that Dr. Stakic himself participated in the entire joint criminal enterprises during the entire time, or is it possible for the Office of the Prosecutor to limit within these dates, October 1991, Dayton 1995, the period of time where it's the alleged responsibility of Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is. That's a matter of evidence as opposed to pleading. Your Honour, we're alleging his participation in a single joint enterprise. So that's what's pleaded in the indictment. We're not for one moment suggesting that up until the Dayton accords Dr. Stakic was playing a part in it. I can't now without looking at the dates look at when he was no longer in power. But clearly, when he was no longer in power, he had no ability to do anything within the joint enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, one has to balance the interests I hear of the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence, and to be honest, I wouldn't regard it as a question of evidence only; it's a question for which period of time the accused is held responsible, and to prepare his own Defence, I believe it's necessary --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. If Your Honour looks at the counts, Your Honour will see the period. That's the period. That's the period for which we're holding him liable, so between the 30th of April, 1992, and the 30th of September, 1992. That's in the counts itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I appreciate very much this clarification, and probably it helps also for the Defence a better understanding of what was said in the motion objecting the form of this third indictment. And I think from the side of the Office of the Prosecutor we have all the necessary clarifications. And it's now to turn to the Defence counsel. I can guarantee you that we extremely carefully read your contributions on the question of the form of this third indictment. And of course, we are prepared to make a clear and precise decision on this issue. But when it comes to the merits of your contribution, I believe most clarifications have been given, especially now that on the time limit, what you pointed out correctly in your motion. But to be honest also in your direction, until now we have at least the feeling that most of your other contributions are more ones related really to questions of evidence, of the evaluation. And my direct question is now: When you have heard these clarifications, wouldn't it be in the interest of justice and the expeditious proceedings appropriate for you to withdraw your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was told yesterday on the meeting that you cannot decide on this motion by yourself, that you have to wait to decide with two other ad litem Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I have to admit that I was caught by surprise by this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably you can rethink we will have a break. But you can -- as I mentioned before, you can take it really as granted that it was already discussed, of course no decision was made until now. But it was discussed, and this -- the points we mentioned -- I mentioned until now were the points that we found there were some merits in your contribution and they needed clarification. But personally I believe we have got this clarification now, and I can't expect an immediate answer. Probably after the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay, then just give me time until next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, an apropos break. Was it possible for you, Dr. Stakic, to discuss with your Defence counsel the question whether or not you are prepared to consent, that in the absence of the one or the other Defence counsel, we can continue with one Defence counsel alone? THE ACCUSED STAKIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I had time to consult my counsel, and I agree with this proposal given by my Defence counsel which would allow just one of the Defence counsel to be present during trial if we are talking about a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. We may now turn to the question of witnesses. There is first of all the question, the status of each witness. We'll say viva voce witnesses, 92 bis witnesses, deposition to be taken, videolink to be used. As to the fact that these witnesses have been put down at various stages as different times as witnesses, I would regard it as rather helpful if we just could go through the list of witnesses. I believe the last entire list of witnesses was one in your motion of 28 March. It was a decision of 28 March, and your list was from 14 of March, 2002, where we start with Witness Number 1 as a 92 bis witness. If you please, I don't want to mention the names. If you could yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I haven't at the moment got a copy. I didn't know that Your Honour was going to go through the list, so I'm afraid I didn't bring it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be possible later on this afternoon to go through this list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour would put this off until after the next break, and I'll get the list then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fine. Then what about the list of the first ten witnesses in trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've today filed confidentially and provided to Mr. Lukic this afternoon a copy of the first ten -- the names of the first ten witnesses. We can hand Your Honour a copy now, but it has been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could. You have got the list, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Is it agreed between the parties that the Office of the Prosecutor will provide the Defence and the Chamber with a list of the coming witnesses one week in advance?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're perfectly prepared to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yesterday, as I understood it correctly, it was not quite clear whether or not there should be a provisional, emphasise, provisional, list of all witnesses in the order envisaged by the OTP at this stage before we enter trial. I know there are numerous ifs and buts, deposition, 92 bis, but it would be really helpful for us if we could have such a provisional list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The difficulty, Your Honour, is this: That because of the overlap between this case and the Brdjanin/Talic case, not in the sense of the witnesses but lawyers, it's sometimes quite difficult to work out, because certain lawyers have to call certain witnesses in advance who is going to be doing what, and that's why we prefer not to do this quite honestly. It isn't so much the fact that we know roughly which way we want to run it, but it may be because of the lawyer crossover there's a problem. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably later on when we have hopefully some solution on the motion on depositions, we can more clearly proceed and find out what is realistic. utterances.text: Let us now turn to one of the most crucial issues of this case, and this is, of course, a question how to resolve the problem of witnesses being witnesses, viva voce witnesses, apparently, in both cases Brdjanin/Talic and Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me for interrupting you. I just have one issue regarding this list of ten first witnesses, so I plea to go back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please. Take the floor, please, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying together with the Prosecution office to solve the problem of the first witness, expert witness, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I now myself interrupt you. Of course, I will come back to Dr. Donia later this afternoon when we come to the programme of the first four days, the start of the trial in a broader sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, no problem. Now, the most crucial problem is, of course, that we have apparently ten witnesses parallel in both cases, Brdjanin/Talic and Stakic. I think at the present time, we shouldn't think back annoyed about the development the cases have taken since 1997 or 1999. I would invite all the parties to look just in the future and to come to solutions of the future. We all were involved in difficult discussions how to resolve the problem, how in the best way, how to avoid that witnesses have to come twice or even more times when it comes later to other cases where these witness statements are necessary. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this matter was discussed yesterday with Your Honour's senior legal officer. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Until now, as I mentioned, we had already some discussions between the Judges in both cases, and of course we have not only to face -- I don't want to call it the problem, but the objections of Defence counsel to this idea of taking depositions. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The difficulty, Your Honour, is this: If, for example, you look at the list. I'll just find it myself. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Isn't it true that the same obstacle you correctly mentioned before, that some witnesses can't be heard already now in Brdjanin/Talic because the disclosure is not ripe for all this, and the Defence is not prepared, that this indeed would be true in case we take depositions, and then of course the Defence counsel in Brdjanin/Talic would argue, we need, first of all, the supporting material in order to be prepared for the cross-examination. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I absolutely agree. Your Honour, I'm not pursuing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this. I mean, it's a dead -- dead in the water, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.text: Unfortunately. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I should point out to Your Honour that these eight witnesses were selected because they were not vital for either case. Just to revisit this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, when I say not of value, Your Honour, they are of value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Added.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's simply that, for example, number 3 on the proposed deposition list, you know, is one -- he's unique in one sense. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are certainly important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And therefore I would invite you to rethink whether or not there isn't superior probative value when we would have a deposition taken, for example, in Banja Luka, and there having the cross-examination of these two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In respect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It can't be resolved today I'm quite sure, but we have to consider all the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. But the innovative suggestions that have been made don't seem to be meeting with much favour with anybody in this place. Witness Number 3 is somebody we would certainly wish Your Honours to see personally, and that's... On Witness number 7, it's less important, but on Witness Number 3, it would be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you go to the library and find out what the superior probative value is, videolink witness be heard and seen by all the Judges of the Bench, or to have at least one Judge and the Defence counsel and a representative of the OTP present close to this witness, and have the personal impression, once again, the question of body language, this can never be transported by the means of videolink even if it's of extreme good quality. But there is really a discussion, and I regard it now as a majority in the opinion of our learned friends that the better way to have these witnesses is when they are heard by deposition instead of this poor and weak videolink version. I don't believe that you really succeed in that what you want to give us the real, the live impression, of this witness via videolink. There, the experiences of the past, even though there were extremely good conditions, they were rather poor. So therefore, this should be resolved, and of course we come back to this point. But in principle, the solution of Judge Agius and mine was to ask you to find, if possible, a solution bringing us a separate hearing of the witnesses, if possible, and probably we can make once again is the distinction in the list of the ten when we go through witness by witness. But this shouldn't be done today. This should be done only when we have the entire Bench here present. Therefore, I would invite you to rethink it now. But we have to come back to this next week. Yes, now, I have to turn to a very crucial point of the exchange of our visions and confessions as regards, first of all, the identification procedure. I think we all have got your point in your motion, and no doubt, this, if you so want, this has to be done. There has to be a presentation of excellent photographs. So no doubt. But when it comes to the recognition of a person, I think we all agree that it has no probative value at all to come to this as it is called in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, "the courtroom identification" because if there is one person in the courtroom and another person in the colour of the United Nations beside, it's quite clear it's a person. It was decided in some other cases. But working on such a case, this brought me to the problem and how to resolve the problem that indeed, we don't have any rules on recognition and how to do this in the most favourable way. For example, as it is foreseen in most countries, I don't think it's a question of common law or civil law in this case, that there is an additional value when you really proceed with a lineup or as it is called in the United States, an identification parade, Blacks, seventh edition. Then you can find it's really some practical experience when we come to this point. I understand that these two witnesses you mentioned in your motion are extremely important for the case. And therefore, we shouldn't hesitate to exhaust all the possibilities to come as close as possible to the truth. And my question is really, why not try to find out whether there is another solution, another result, when we have additionally, emphasise additionally, such a very formal identification parade? Because here, once again, in the literature, you can read a lot about this added value, because it's not only the face, it's not only the beard or whatever, it's also a question of body language and other criteria available only in the framework of such an identification parade. And therefore, I really would ask you to rethink whether it's not better to have additionally such an identification parade as regards these two witnesses, probably by the way of taking depositions, applying the rules on depositions correspondingly, or even in courtroom. This is, of course, the question you have to answer, what seems to be more appropriate for you. But to the point, all possibilities have to be exhausted to come as close as possible to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I understand Your Honour correctly, and I want to make sure that I do, you would like the two witnesses who say "we knew Stakic, and we saw him in a certain place and recognised him because of our previous relation with him" nonetheless, you would like an identification parade to be held at which they should attend to see whether they can identify him now, ten years after, with a beard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Supposing, Your Honour, they don't? Is Your Honour going to treat their evidence as less value because ten years on, they don't recognise him, and because he looks completely different from -- and no doubt about it, he looks completely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, not in the framework of this Tribunal. But in numerous domestic courts, I can here unfortunately more refer to jurisprudence and the factual situation in the Russian federation than in Germany. There have been some discussions in the federations on this issue, and normally it is conducted this way to do both, and even if one fails, it doesn't mean that the witness does not recognise this person. It could be, for example, there is a recognition on the basis of different photos, and this could be under the free evolution of evidence enough to come to a conclusion. Or the other way around: During an identification parade, for reasons you can never foresee, there is an identification because suddenly a person asked to recognise another person finds out, oh, now I remember. This is the reason why I really can remember this was the person. And so therefore, to do it twice is better than to omit one possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour. I understand. That's why I asked Your Honour -- forgive me for asking Your Honour the question. It may well be that they do recognise him. It may well be that they all never forget his face, even disguised as it is with a beard. Not disguised but the change. Equally they may not. And that's why I'm saying it's unfair, in our submission, on the witness to ask him to do this. Now, of course, if there is a dispute that these witnesses genuinely did recognise him, then clearly we must make what attempts we can. But then I think the fairest way of doing it is to take a photograph of what he looked like then, take another half a dozen photographs or however many Your Honour thinks right, and ask them to pick him. It may not be known to Your Honour but in the United Kingdom, you are not allowed to hold dock identifications under any circumstances because there have been too many mistakes or that's what the courts thought. And one of the things is if there is recognition, so called, then there is an identification parade held. But not ten years after the event, and not -- that's the unfairness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think we should use the notion of unfairness vis-a-vis any party or vis-a-vis as a witness, because it seems to be quite clear that it is extremely difficult to recognise and then identify a person ten years after an alleged incident. But one should at least try. And as I mentioned already, the literature I worked on on this issue in the past when preparing the Russian code of criminal procedures, we went into these details, and surprisingly the results of these attempts, suddenly even 20, 25 years after an incident, people, for the one or other reason, can recognise a person during an identification parade. And therefore, really, I would recommend to do this, and I regard this as my duty bearing in mind the Kupreskic decision where it was clearly stated that it was for the Judges to take care that all evidence is brought to the attention of the Chamber and that we have to use all evidence and all possible means of evidence taking. And therefore, it's just my recommendation to do both, and not only to do what evidently is necessary to provide the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we've certainly heard what Your Honour says. Apart from the practical difficulties of how you hold an identification parade in the detention unit, that's another matter. I don't think we're discussing practical matters here. Your Honour, we certainly have heard what your going to say. It may assist however, I think, if -- I would certainly invite Mr. Lukic to indicate whether there is going to be a dispute, that these two particular witnesses knew Stakic and could recognise him. Because I think that would assist, and then obviously we will have to consider everything Your Honour says about how we deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Lukic, what is your position to this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, I haven't confirmed with my client yet whether these persons know him or not. First of all, I have to check who these persons are. But I know what they should confirm. But anyway, we would ask the Court to halt any pictures from this courtroom to go outside of Mr. Stakic from now on, before this recognition has been done, or will be done. Because I know in Omarska case, we had people who would say we don't have TV. And we know that they even discussed about the pictures. We knew it from the other witnesses. So everybody is looking, this programme, and everybody is following these trials. So we are quite sure that those two witnesses which should recognise the accused will follow the trial of reports. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this contribution. But unfortunately, in our media society, it is not possible at all if only once a picture is out, then it is on the market. And we can't prevent anybody to produce new copies from these photos in the future. And what we should not do today is to try to already evaluate what will be probably in the future. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course. Only what I have to state is that if the pictures go out from this courtroom, it would give us a good foundation for any kind of objections to the recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm fully aware of this. But just in the past, I saw in two different newspapers the picture of Dr. Stakic, and we can't stop this process unfortunately. And therefore, protective measures are not helpful indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take Mr. Lukic's point, and obviously, if we get to the point of identification, we'll ask the witnesses whether they have watched, they have seen any of the proceedings. But I don't think, Your Honour, it would be right to stop proceedings going out for an issue like this. I think, Your Honour, the answer is for the moment, we've understood Your Honour's concerns, and we'll have to see how things run from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Then we come to another point, the Prosecution's request for a variation of Pre-Trial Judge's order for filing of motions and related matters. If I see this correctly, we have to regard the three motions pending until now as one attempt to clarify open questions during the Pre-Trial. And of course, to be quite clear, both the attempt to come to rules or guidelines on the admissibility of evidence or other related questions, this can't be -- can't form part of an order of a Pre-Trial Judge, no doubt. But as there were no objections from both parties, when it comes to the question of the admissibility of evidence, there will be a decision already in the beginning of next week, because this point seems to be undisputed between the parties. What indeed seems to be disputed, probably even this is not the case, is the question of the right of the accused to speak out during the trial. Of course, once again, this is only a suggestion until now, and it's for the Judges in future to decide on this issue. But only to decide on this issue when it's really a relevant problem. From my point of view, it becomes only then for the Office of the Prosecutor a relevant problem if it really is the case that Dr. Stakic requests to take the floor, and the floor is granted; and in addition, the Office of the Prosecutor sees some prejudice in this. But here, once again, we have to clearly distinguish between different notions. It is, of course, not the question of testifying at all; it's a question whether or not an accused has a right to make a statement. This is not the question of testimony during the trial. I understand that the Office of the Prosecutor wants to make the point that this is not allowed under our Rules because until now, it's only the possibility explicitly for seeing that there is either testimony - we don't discuss testimonies - or an opening statement. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. And the Office of the Prosecutor took the liberty to address in paragraph 10 apples and pears in one and the same paragraph when quoting Judge Agius. I discussed this issue with Judge Agius and of course the point Judge Agius made was only on testimony and not on statements. And in addition, quite right, in the Rules explicitly, and it's mandatory, that the right has to be given for a statement in the beginning. But of course, this is not limited from a human rights perspective. Of course the accused always enjoys the right to make statements, not to testify, to make statements, as it was done, for example, in Kunarac appeal case. The Judges decided that it is necessary to have an additional statement, so-called last word, to be granted to the accused. You will never find this in the Rules. But it is inherent, as it is the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, all our Rules and the Statutes has of course to be read in the light of human right norms. And there, it was clearly held always in the past that it's undoubtedly the right for the accused to speak to the Judges, if he so wants, because he is the main person. He is not the subject -- he's not the object of the proceedings; he is, indeed, the subject with own rights. And what my intention indeed was, and therefore I was surprised to get objections from the side of the Office of the Prosecutor, to limit these rights of the accused to certain points in time for the order of a correct trial, not to disturb witnesses, but saying that it would be an appropriate point in time for the accused to give his assessment in the form of a statement of a witness testimony. When a witness has left this room, then it should be the right for the accused to give a short assessment, if he so wants, if he so wants, on this evidence we all just heard. And I can tell you by experience, it's in addition helpful in the assessment of a witness statement to hear immediately the reaction if an accused so wants of the accused, because later on during the last word, it's difficult to come back and to remind us on these issues. And therefore, I regard this as a limitation of the inherent rights of the witness, rather than granting new rights. And you made several points under paragraph 8 of your statement. You asked the question on what aspect he may testify? As I mentioned, it's not a question of testifying, but rather a statement. Just the evidence given by the witness, or matters related to this testimony? It's only to give the possibility, if he so wants, to prepare his own assessment, as I said before. Next bullet: "Will the testimony be under solemn declaration?" No, of course not, it's a statement, and the rules of statement and the probative value of statements apply correspondingly. Next bullet: "Will the accused be asked questions by his counsel or merely make a statement at whatever lengths he chooses?" Of course no questions by the counsel because when the counsel wants to speak, it's all right for the counsel to do this but not to ask questions at this point in time, as it is said in the rules governing statements, there is no question of the accused at this point in time at all. And it is of course, not whatever length he chooses. It is only to the points relevant to the statement we all together heard just before. Of course, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence will be allowed to cross-examine or to re-examine the accused, and the Judges will have not the right to put questions to the accused. It's really the own statement. But to come back to the central point, I think we really can wait whether or not the accused will make use of this inherent right in future, and then if the OTP really so wants, then we should discuss their objections. Probably it's a fight on -- I don't want to go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's probably exceedingly academic because I have already discussed this matter with Mr. Lukic. And Mr. Lukic has an American co-counsel, and I have no doubt at all that the advice that will given to Dr. Stakic is that he shouldn't open his mouth. But as a matter of principle, it is I think the real difference between a system whereby the Judges effectively ask all the questions of witnesses at whatever stage they like, and a system whereby evidence is given by witnesses being called by counsel and cross-examined by counsel. And the Rule is absolutely, in our submission, clear. And Your Honour says a muddling statement as testifying. There is no such thing as a difference here between a statement and testifying. A statement is testimony. The weight of the testimony, if we look at Rule 84, it says: "The accused may after the opening statement of the Prosecutor" so it sets out a very clear delineation, "if he or she wishes, and the Trial Chamber so decides, make a statement under the control of the Trial Chamber. The accused shall not be compelled to make a solemn declaration, and shall not be examined about the content of the statement. And the Trial Chamber shall decide on the probative value." Your Honour, I don't want to enter into the rights and wrongs of the two systems, civil and common law. I say that it's simply the rule, and the rule makes it absolutely clear. If the accused wants to make a statement, then it should be made after the opening statement of the Prosecutor. If they wanted to say he could make it any time, they would have said it. Your Honour, if the Judges decide to change the Rules because they agree with Your Honour's definition, then we have no objection. All we're saying is that as a matter of the Statute and the Rules, he doesn't have the right to make a statement as and when he wants to. He has a right to make the statement after the opening statement of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you then say that it was a breach of the Rules conducted by the Appeals Chamber in Kunarac to granting the last word, the granting of the possibility of a statement at the end of the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it wasn't a trial, it was an appeal. I'm afraid I haven't read the Kunarac judgement recently, and I didn't recall that they had asked the accused to make a statement. But the reason that this is in here is because of the very points that we raised in paragraph 8, that there is a need for an orderly progression of evidence, and that evidence is called on behalf of the Prosecution, and then on behalf of the Defence. Your Honour, it seriously does raise all sorts of difficulties that we have set out if the defendant is given the right to say what he likes at the end of each witness, or whatever they feel like presumably as well. The end result could also be that the defendant never has to go into the witness box to give any sort of evidence at all because he has effectively given it through these [indiscernible] statements which Your Honour is bound to take into account. Your Honour, as I say, it may well be that it is purely academic, and it may be that Your Honour is entitled -- obviously entitled -- to leave this matter in abeyance until a request is made. All that we're saying, this is not something that the Rules do allow for, in our submission. And if Your Honour decides, because there is a request, that Your Honour will give permission, then our remedy is to appeal Your Honour's ruling. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course, quite clear. utterances.text: I don't think there is a problem on this point, no. So then we -- you fixed or you said the approximate date to testify for this other witness would be 18 to 21 April. That would bring us to Monday. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Including cross-examination or?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was -- we estimated including cross-examination. As I say, the first two witnesses are likely to be the lengthier ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Parties should be aware that on Friday, there is only a limited time available for us. But probably, it will be possible, nevertheless, to conclude the 21st. I just wanted to make this point, so nobody is surprised when we stop on Friday a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I think we had forgotten, or I know there has been a change. But isn't it right, there's a plenary on the 23rd, so the courts won't be sitting on the Tuesday? I just noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is right, indeed. This would bring us to 21 April. And then just to be on the safe side, what is planned for the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why we skipped the 22nd. I think we are just going on with a witness. I think maybe our dates were slightly wrong there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness Number 3, Number 45 would be present already?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Or in fact, it may well that be the Defence will be ready to cross-examine Dr. Donia then, on the Monday, the 22nd, depending on -- I have to sort this out with the Galic team. I don't know what they have got planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 22nd. Now, back from 26 to 22nd. But I really think it's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. He has to leave. Dr. Donia is actually leaving on the 26th. That was why I mentioned the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's envisage to have the 22nd for the cross-examination and for all the questions the Judges may have on this issue. utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Your Honour -- may I say that Mr. Cayley, who is not really involved in this case, is going to be calling him. And I haven't really discussed the length of the testimony. I think the idea is to very briefly flesh out the sort of general background, and then go straight into Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good. Then, I believe we should not attempt to go on further with the detailed planning of the next days. Then I would understand that the next witness would appear the 24th, 25th, and 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is the witness that I really would like to try and get some arrangement made with the Brdjanin/Talic case because, as I say, he has testified already here three times. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This would then bring us to 24, if it's possible, 24, 25, 26 April. In the past, and if I understood it correctly, also yesterday, you made the point that it would be approximately -- the envisaged time would be approximately three months?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's our best estimate of the Prosecution case, including cross-examination of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So there could be a best-case scenario that we could probably conclude your case before the summer Court recess starting the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If everything proceeded smoothly and there were no breaks -- well, I wouldn't say there's a good chance. There's a realistic prospect of concluding the Prosecution case by August.

utterances.text: Let's try our best, all the participants. Okay. Thank you for reminding me that there is -- there was still one open point, to go through the witness list.

utterances.text: It's your plan to proceed on this basis.
